context.heading: Paneled houses
context.body: The people lived in saphan ("paneled") houses (v. 4), the word used for the cedar paneling of Solomon's temple and palace (1 Kings 6:9; 7:3). Wood paneling was a luxury in a land short of timber. They had found money for finishing touches at home while God's house sat as a ruin.

context.heading: Wages in a leaky purse
context.body: Verse 6 ends with wages dropped into a bag naqav ("pierced" with holes). Coins were carried in cloth pouches; a torn one meant money vanished without a trace. Failed harvests and drought fit the covenant warnings of Deuteronomy 28:38–40, which these returned exiles would have known.

context.heading: Each running to his own
context.body: In verse 9 the people are each ruts ("running") to their own house. The word suggests hurry and urgency. They were not lazy; they were busy. The problem was not effort but direction.

theology.title: A God who speaks through scarcity
theology.body: The LORD connects empty barns and short paychecks to misplaced priorities. Not every hardship is a message about our choices (Job and John 9:3 warn against that assumption), but here God says plainly that He is using lack to call His people back to Himself.

theology.title: "I am with you"
theology.body: Once the people obey, God's whole message is two words in Hebrew: "I am with you" (v. 13). It is the promise given to Moses, Joshua and Jeremiah, and the name given to Jesus, Immanuel (Matthew 1:23). He ends His Great Commission with the same words (Matthew 28:20).

theology.title: He stirs the spirit
theology.body: Verse 14 says the LORD stirred the spirit of leaders and people alike. Their obedience was real, but it was God who woke them up, and within 24 days they were at work. Renewal begins with Him, even when we are the ones who pick up the tools (Philippians 2:13).

application.title: "Not yet the time"
application.body: The people did not refuse to build; they just kept postponing (v. 2). "Later" is often the most respectable way to say no to God.
application.question: What have you been telling God "not yet" about for longer than you would like to admit?

application.title: Holes in the bag
application.body: Earning more did not help, because the money kept leaking away. Sometimes the problem is not income but what we are building with it.
application.question: Where does your money seem to disappear without leaving anything that matters?

context.heading: Treasures or the Desired One
context.body: Verse 7 says the nations' chemdah ("treasures" or "desired things") will come. Older translations read "the desire of all nations shall come", which many took as a title for the Messiah. The Hebrew verb is plural, so most modern versions read "treasures". Either way, God promises to fill this humble house with glory.

context.heading: Holiness does not rub off
context.body: The priests' ruling in verses 12–13 is precise: consecrated meat does not make what it touches holy, but contact with a corpse makes things unclean. Haggai's point is that being near the temple did not make a careless people holy, while their sin was contaminating all they offered.

context.heading: The Spirit remains
context.body: God says His ruach ("Spirit") "remains among you" (v. 5), linking the small rebuilding project to the exodus, when His presence led Israel in cloud and fire. The same God who went with them out of Egypt was standing with these builders.

theology.title: Greater glory in a smaller house
theology.body: The second temple was plainer than Solomon's, yet God said its latter glory would be greater (v. 9). Herod later enlarged it, but its true glory came when Jesus walked its courts, taught there and called His own body the temple (John 2:19–21).

theology.title: One more shaking
theology.body: Hebrews 12:26–28 quotes verse 6: God will shake heaven and earth once more, so that only what cannot be shaken remains. Haggai pictured nations and thrones being overturned (v. 22). The kingdom believers receive in Christ is the one thing that will still be standing.

theology.title: The chosen servant
theology.body: Zerubbabel, a descendant of David, is called God's servant and signet ring (v. 23). He never ruled as king, but he appears in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:12–13; Luke 3:27). God kept David's line alive for the King still to come.

application.title: Do not despise the smaller version
application.body: Some wept because the new temple looked like nothing compared with the old (v. 3). Comparing with "the good old days" can drain the strength we need for today's work.
application.question: What good work in front of you are you discounting because it is smaller than what used to be?

application.title: Work, for I am with you
application.body: God's command in verse 4 is simple: be strong and work. His presence is not a reason to sit back but the reason to pick up the tools.
application.question: What task have you been waiting to feel ready for that you should just start this week?
